## Synthesized Text

There is a quiet asymmetry at the heart of measuring any moving system. The funded survey is precise and rare. The amateur observation is noisy and constant. We are trained to trust the first and dismiss the second — and for measuring a *state*, that instinct is right. But almost nothing we care about is a state. It is a *change*. And change is caught by frequency, not by precision.

TidePool is a small wager on this asymmetry. A tide pool appears for two hours, twice a day, and then is gone. No research budget can be everywhere it appears. But ten thousand people already walk those flats with cameras in their pockets — the observation is going to happen regardless. The only question is whether the signal is thrown away. Make the photo the logging act, and a coastline becomes an instrument that no grant could fund.

The deeper pattern generalizes past tide pools. Any time an act people already perform can be turned, frictionlessly, into a logged signal, you can out-measure a better-funded effort that has to *manufacture* its observations. The walk, the commute, the purchase, the search — these are happening anyway. Coverage is cheap when you stop trying to create it and start trying to *capture* it.
